en: [When Makaranda has been married to Nandana under the mistaken impression that he is Mālatī, the play begins the act following the events therein.

Buddharakṣitā: Ah! Makaranda has been safely protected by the arrangements of the venerable lady in the house of Minister Bhūrivasu; there, his hand was taken by Nandana, who was deceived by the splendor of Mālatī’s attire. "Ah! expresses both great joy and wonder. "Protected" (gopāyita): he was not observed by anyone.
"Today we have come to this residence in the Nandana grove. Therefore, the Blessed Lady has taken leave of Nandana and gone to her own quarters.

*Āpṛcchya* means having held a conversation with him, having performed such a form of address as: "O noble Nandana, I am departing; may you grant me your permission. (1) *Āvasatham* means a house; the sense is "her own.
Furthermore, this evening—during which the entire retinue is distracted and confused by the great festival of the *akālakaumudī* celebrated upon the entry of a new bride—will favor our undertaking.
The sense is that, while the attendants are occupied elsewhere, the union of Makaranda with Madayantikā will occur without obstacle at nightfall.

Now indeed, the son-in-law—his amorous passion being urgent, unable to endure delay—having repeatedly entreated her to love him with prostrations at her feet, and then having rushed upon her by force, was harshly repulsed by Makaranda.
"Urgent passion" (*tvaramāṇakāma*) means one whose surge of love cannot tolerate any delay.

With his voice faltering and his face quivering with suppressed sobs, his silence broken by a torrent of rage, he made a vow with oaths, saying, "I have no further need of you, a harlot from your youth," and departed from the bedchamber; taking advantage of this incident, I shall bring Madayantika here and unite her with Makaranda.

"One whose tone falters along with his syllables" means that his speech has an indistinguishable division of phonemes and a produced variation in pitch. "Filled with rage," and for that very reason, "stammering" (*khuḍuṃkita*). Those learned in poetry say that stammering is silence as well as the contraction of the mouth. (2) Likewise, "weeping" (*oruṇṇa*) means having wept; that is to say, with tears in the eyes. "One whose face is quivering" is so described. "A harlot from childhood" (*kaumārabandhakī*) means a prostitute. "Occasion" (*prasaṅga*) means an arrangement or a plan.

Because entering while asleep is forbidden according to the *Bharata* [treatise], he says, "having gone to bed. (3) [Makaranda: "I hope" (*api nāma*) expresses a possibility. The policy of the Blessed Lady has been transferred to Buddharakṣitā: a web of village-encounters with Madayantika.

(4) Lavaṅgikā: What doubt can there be for the noble sir? What need is there for much talk? Just as this sound of anklets is, so do I know that Madayantika has been brought here by Buddharakṣitā under that pretext. Therefore, remain concealed by your upper garment, appearing as if asleep. [00]

*Mañjīram*: an anklet. *Tena vyapadeśena*: under the pretext of reproaching Mālatī, who had angered her brother. *Suptalakṣaḥ*: "sleep" is *suptam*; that is the *lakṣa*, i.e., the pretext, which he has—thus [he is so called]. Or rather: "stay in such a way that you appear as if asleep.
MADAYANTIKĀ: Friend, is it truly the case that my brother has been provoked by Mālatī? BUDDHARAKṢITĀ: Indeed so.
The meaning is "just so. MĀDAYANTIKĀ: Alas, what a calamity!
An action that disregards one's life is called a calamity (*atyāhita*).
Therefore, come, let us reproach the ill-behaved Mālatī.
Buddharakṣitā: This is the door to the bedchamber.
Madayantikā: Friend Lavaṅgikā, it is known that your dear friend is fast asleep.

"It is known; it is apparent. LĀVAGIKĀ: "Do not wake her; she has been despondent for a long time and has only just now fallen into a light sleep. Therefore, sit down quietly right here on this half of the couch.
*Maṇiaṃ*: slightly; for a shorter duration. *Saṇiaṃ*: slowly."

MADAYANTIKĀ: Why is this woman of perverse character so dejected? LAVAṄGIKĀ: How could our dear friend not be dejected upon obtaining as her husband your brother, who knows the means of winning a young bride’s confidence, who is charming, clever, sweet-spoken, and free from anger?

*Viśrambhaṇam*: winning over by producing confidence. *Laḍaham*: one endowed with qualities such as fresh youth. *Vidagdham*: one who is expert in the matters concerning the union with a maiden. [00] Thus, there is a three-word *karmadhāraya* compound. [00] As for the means of winning the confidence of a new bride, there are worldly methods for attracting a maiden, such as "The young girl is to be won over by betel, garlands, the juice of fruits, delicious food, and honor," and so forth.
[00] And the intention regarding all these adjectives is that they serve as counter-examples (*pratyudāharaṇa*) for Nandana.
MADAYANTIKĀ: Look, Buddharakṣitā! We are being reproached for acting contrary to what is right.
"Acting contrary" (vipratīpa) means "inverted," because we are not deserving of reproach. BUDDHARAKṢITĀ: It is either contrary or it is not contrary. [00]

First, with the hidden intention that she speaks only what is appropriate because she has consented to the contrary position out of a desire to comply with his mind, he asks: "Is it so? [00] MĀDAYANTIKĀ: "How so?
BUDDHARAKṢITĀ, however, in order to conceal her own true state of mind, explains her own words by focusing on the fact that the reproach applies equally to both of them.

First, as for the fact that my husband was not highly esteemed here because he bowed at her feet—this person [myself] is to be blamed for the fault of shame. Furthermore, regarding whatever improper words were uttered by your brother—which betrayed his noble character due to the embarrassment of a sudden lapse in conduct contrary to the nature of a young bride—it is for this reason that you [are addressed] in such a manner.

While it should have been said that "this woman is to be censured," the expression "this person" was used by Buddharakṣitā out of her cleverness, applying it without distinction to both man and woman. As for the commencement of sexual union with a newlywed bride, done impulsively—that is, through an unexamined perception of beauty and merely out of the pride of ownership—it is "contrary," meaning it is not auspicious. For it has been said: "If a maiden is approached impulsively by one who has not won her heart, she immediately experiences fear, terror, agitation, and even hatred."

"Having failed to attain union with joy, she was corrupted by that agitation; she might either become a hater of men, or, being repelled, go to another. Thus [is the definition]. From that, "stumbling" (*skhalana*) occurs: the failure to carry through what has been commenced. From that, "embarrassment" (*vailakṣya*): a lack of resolution. By that, "scattered" (*vicchardita*): dispersed here and there, is the "greatness of nature" (*mahānubhāvatva*), which is the quality of having an excellent character. "Reached by speech" means "pertaining to speech" (*vāggata*). Non-abiding (*aparisthāna*):

The absence of *paristhāpanā*—that is, the stabilization of a settled state (*paristhiti*). This amounts to a lack of fortitude (*adhairya*); for they say that fortitude is the supreme station of a leader. The address "you are to be reproached" is directed at Madayantikā because, by belonging to her brother's faction, she is included within that category. In the reading *amhe*, Buddharakṣitā, wishing to express her non-difference from Madayantikā, says "we. *Anadhigata* means trust; that is, familiarity firmly established, [the lack of which] pertains to those [whom one addresses]. *Saṃprayoga* refers to internal sexual union.
Thus, indeed, the authors of the *Kāmasūtra* declare.

LĀVANGIKĀ: In every house, men marry girls of good family, yet no one—by means of the fire of their words, claiming "I am the master"—ignites with the flames of their speech those innocent young women of noble birth whose very nature is modesty and innocence. These are indeed great humiliations, like the implanting of a thorn in the heart, which remain unbearable as long as they are remembered until death, causing a distaste for living in the houses of others; it is for the sake of these that kinsmen loathe the very attainment of birth as a woman. MADAYANTIKĀ: She is distressed; she is tormented. Therefore.
Buddharakṣitā, my dear friend Lavaṅgikā has been greatly tormented. Has some very great offense been committed by my brother? Buddharakṣitā:
Indeed so; that is exactly what it means.
"We have indeed heard that you currently have no need for me, a discarded maiden from my youth.

MADAYANTIKĀ: Oh, what an insult! Oh, what a transgression! Friend Lavaṅgikā, I am now unable even to look you in the face. Nevertheless, since I still possess some power, I shall say something. "I possess power"—even as the sister of a son-in-law, I feel encouraged toward you by the force of our affection.
Lāvaṅgikā: "This person is at your disposal;

tell me what you wish," is the meaning. Mādayantikā: "You have already seen for yourselves my brother's lack of character and his conduct; yet even one such as this must now be followed according to your wishes, since he is your husband."

And that which was seen as the basis for immorality is precisely this. And it is "presently," because there is no other possible state once marriage has taken place. Nor do you fail to know the root of this acquisition of reproach consisting of impure syllables and insults.
"Anabhijātākṣara" means one whose syllables are impure (*aśuddhākṣara*). "Adhikṣepa" means reviling (*nirbhartsana*); "lambha" of that is its acquisition (*prāpti*).
Lāvaṅgikā: How is it that we do not even know what has been said?
We do indeed know what was said; however, the meaning is that it is merely heard as something brought forth by those words.

Madayantikā: Regarding that certain affection for Tārā which Mālatī reportedly felt toward the highly fortunate Mādhava at that time, there is a rumor concerning it that has reached the highest pitch among all people. That rumor is spreading in this way: "O dear friend, act in such a way that this husband’s partiality toward [another] is completely uprooted from his heart."

Otherwise, let it be known that this is a great negligence; indeed, such a wicked attachment causes a heartless and cruel affliction to the hearts of men toward women. Thinking, "This maiden is in love with another man," the distress that arises in the hearts of men becomes firm, and for that very reason, it becomes cruel. This "wicked attachment" (*durabhiṣvaṅga*) refers to an improper attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*), which is to say, a passionate obsession (*anurāgābhiniveśa*) resulting from a connection with another man. Do not say, "It was not told by Madayantikā."
Lāvaṅgikā: Noble sir, you are deluded by the confused talk of the world; begone, for I will not converse with you.

Mādayantikā: Friend, be gracious, or rather, you have not been told clearly. Stay! Do we not know that Mālatī’s entire world of living beings consists solely of Mādhava? And who else could have brought about her extraordinary beauty—beauty produced by the emaciation of her limbs, which possess the grace of the interior of a mature *ketakī* flower—and who else could have provided the sole means of her survival, namely the *vakula*-garland fashioned by Mādhava’s own hand and worn around her neck?

In this context, the completion of the sentence occurs through the connection with what is to be said next: "the body has not been perceived. *Racitam* means "made" or "constructed. *Avalambanam* means "support.
(15) And as for Mādhava’s body—its appearance lovely, slightly emaciated, and pale like the orb of the morning moon—has it not been perceived?
*Kim* is used here in the sense of a question. The word *taddivasa* refers to that specific time. (16)

Moreover, when they met at the entrance of the street bordering the Kusumākarodyāna garden that day, their faces blossoming with the haste of curiosity and playful radiance—those glances of theirs, charmingly sweet and full of artistry fashioned by the most diligent instruction of the dance-master of the Bodiless One (Kāma), wherein the pupils trembled with graceful and smooth beauty—were not observed even by me.

*Paryantaḥ* means *parisaraḥ* (the vicinity). Those two whose faces were *praphulla*—that is, blossomed or opened wide—by that *halapphaliyā*, which is haste characterized by a playful and shimmering curiosity. [00] The word "no" (*na*) is connected with the word "why" (*kim*). And why were the collisions of our glances not observed by me?

Furthermore, having heard the news of my brother’s gift, was the heart of those two—notices of whose bodily splendor was fading, scorched by the onset of a profound agitation arising at that very moment—not perceived to be as if its very roots were being uprooted?

*Āvega* is the suffering of non-attainment. That suffering has "arisen" (*udbhūta*), meaning it has become manifest by abandoning its depth. By the "contact" (*vyatikara*)—that is, the connection—with that suffering, [the heart] is "charred" (*aṅgārita*), meaning it is scorched. "Rising up" (*udvartamāna*) means leaping upward.
(17) Furthermore, this other thing has also been remembered. LAVAṄGIKĀ: What else now?

MADAYANTIKĀ: That which was dear to that noble one who restored my life—namely, the very form of his consciousness—was offered by Mālatī as a report of what she cherished. Upon being awakened by the introduction of the Blessed One’s clever words, my heart and my life were both assigned as a reward for her act of self-choice.
It has been given; this is shown in the verse beginning with "wounded by a beast of prey" (18).
LAVANGIKĀ: O Madayantikā, you yourself said, "Indeed, this favor from our dear friend has been accepted."

*Ā* is used to indicate that a previous form of address has been forgotten. In the reading *aha*, the meaning is "then" (*atha*) or "here" (*atra*). In the reading *alam*, it is a common worldly expression meaning "what else is there to be done here by another?
Lavaṅgikā: Friend, I have almost forgotten who this person of great majesty is. This question is intended precisely to introduce the story once it has been recognized.

MADAYANTIKĀ: Friend, remember how on that day, when I had fallen into the range of a ferocious and enraged wild beast and was without refuge, I was protected by him—my life-giver whose life was as fragile as the tip of a scale-beam—who, acting as a friend without cause, performed the daring act of offering his own body, the sole essence of the entire world, along with his stout pillar-like arms; and who, marked upon his broad, expansive, and fleshy chest...

With a heart solely intent on compassion, he who had stripped away the withered and decayed garland from my head endured for my sake the blows of a falling thunderbolt-like cage formed by the claws of an exceedingly wicked tiger; thus was that evil beast, a great demon, slain. (19)

*Viaḍo*: enraged. *Vinipātaḥ*: a plowshare. *Vibhaktam*: demarcated. *Vikaṭam*: vast. *Māṃsalam*: fleshy. *Uttālam*: a particular state of being situated in a formidable arrangement. *Pariṇāhi*: circular. By the mark upon such a chest. *Jaraṭham*: hard; *jarjaritam*: shattered. "Resembling" (*anuhāri*) refers to the crown fashioned from hibiscus flowers (*javākusuma*). Here, "taking away" (*haraṇa*) means imitation.

And the imitation [of his form] is due to his body being mottled by streams of blood. The blows from the claws of the exceedingly wicked tiger as he falls are themselves the strikes of a cage of thunderbolts. In the reading *nisumbhanta*, the meaning is "being crushed. (20) Because her heart is permeated with intense passion, she does not utter his name out of shame born from the conceit that "this man is my beloved. LAVANGIKĀ: "Hum, it is Makaranda!
"Hum" is used here in a question containing a sense of firm resolve.

MADAYANTIKĀ: Dear friend, what, what do you say? [The repetition of "what" is used here for an emphatic inquiry arising from an excess of joy; for that which is pleasant to hear is heard again and again. Having treated it as if unheard, she makes the repeated statement heard once more. LAVAṄGIKĀ: Indeed, I am saying "Makaranda."
The word *nanu* expresses one's own intention.

[00] "The body" is the subject; the ellipsis to be supplied is "with horripilation produced upon hearing the name Makaranda. You, being thus full of longing for Makaranda, yet regarding Mādhava’s passion for Mālatī as a fault, resemble the story of the bride and the beans, as they say: "The bride measures the beans, yet she does not see her own lower region. (21)

[1] Where one should say "we," the phrase "I" is an expression of wit. Likewise, "so be it" means that it has been accepted that Mālatī is enamored of Mādhava. "What shall I say?"—to whom, who is so obstinate, can anything be said? [00] *Viśuddhaḥ* means stainless (*niṣkalaṅkaḥ*). *Mugdhaḥ* means ignorant of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*). And the recourse to the Sanskrit language is for the sake of jesting, since the attainment of the secret core is not otherwise established, just as in the case of observing the recitation of a *dhruva* verse in a song with great joy. [1]

MADAYANTIKĀ: Friend, why do you mock me? Indeed, I say that even the mention of the name of such a person—one who acted with selfless resolve and rendered a great service by forcibly restoring my life as it was being swallowed by Death—is enough to refresh the soul. (In the reading *nivvāvedi*, it means "it soothes" or "it gladdens. The very restoration of life is the great service.)

And so, you too have witnessed that illustrious man, who—having been momentarily distracted from the onset of the pain of his deep wounds by a surge of perspiration breaking out over his body; whose pair of blue-lotus eyes were closing in a faint; whose bodily weight was supported by the courage provided by leaning on a sword-staff fallen to the ground; and who had surrendered his most precious life-world for the sake of Madayantikā alone.

"Vismāritaśarīrā" (one whose body has been forgotten) is a description of fainting. Its complication is perspiration (*sveda*). "Utpīḍaḥ" means rising up after having become thickened. "Kaṃdoṭṭam" is the blue lotus (*nīlotpala*). By the phrase "merely on account of Madayantikā," [the author] shows his great regard for himself; furthermore, even regarding such a small object, Makaranda’s disregard for himself and his resolute determination—due to both his compassion and his heroism—reveal his greatness. The world of living beings (*jīvaloka*) is of great value because it is attained only with great hardship.
Buddharakṣitā: O you whose body is overcome by trepidation, go away! We have become bold through our familiarity with our co-resident.

The body is dominated by agitation, or rather, the body is agitation itself. We have burst forth: we have been revealed. "Sahavāsinī" means innate (sahajā). Regarding the variant reading: "O friend, even your resolve is manifested in your body. The meaning is that through bodily states such as perspiration and horripilation—which are inseparable from passion—it is evident that union with Makaranda is what you desire.
MADAYANTIKĀ (with shame): Friend, go away! I have been betrayed by the intimacy born of living together.

"I have not broken out in perspiration and so forth out of passion; rather, the meaning is that it was due to the force of confidential conversation with you and my other friends. In this reading, however, the entire subsequent response becomes perfectly coherent.
(23) LAVANGIKĀ: Friend Madayantikā, we too know what ought to be known. Be gracious. Cease from your instruction.
[In the variant reading *apadeśāt*, the meaning is "from the presentation of your own pretext."]
"Come, let us remain in a state that resembles the binding of conversations filled with confidence.

The sense is: you ought to tell all that connection of affection you have toward Makaranda to us, your friends. But as for saying 'cease,' this is your very own path; for what could possibly be told to anyone when you yourself, out of your own independence and under the influence of subsequent passion, are advising against the search for a man?
Buddharakṣitā: Lavangikā speaks well.
MADAYANTIKĀ: Now I am at the service of my dear friends.
LAVAṄGIKĀ: If that is so, then tell us how your time passes.
The meaning is: how do you manage in the absence of Makaranda?
MADAYANTIKĀ: Listen—pay heed.
(25) Dear friend, for my heart was already filled with a longing, curiosity, and desire toward that person, sustained by the conviction of my partiality for Buddharakṣitā.

The conviction (*viśvāsa*) is that Buddharakṣitā’s partiality does not arise without a multitude of manifest virtues; this is the *pratyaya* (cognition). *Uvvarantam*: becoming excessive. (26) The meaning is that curiosity, longing, and desire, having filled the heart, do not fit within it and thus become superabundant. However, some explain it as: that desire in which curiosity and longing have become excessive is so described. [00]

Then, having come to perceive the fulfillment of destiny’s decree, my heart was tormented by the unbearable and fierce suffering of the bodiless god of love; my life-force faltered as my mind yearned [for him], and my attendants became despondent at the sight of the violent and unendurable distress that caused all my limbs to blaze with a previously unknown fire. With my faculties thrown into disorder by the intensification of this possession—fueled by the words of Buddharakṣitā, which were contrary to the extinction of death that is easily obtained through the mere release of hope—I now experience this reversal of the world of the living. (27) *Nirvāṇam*: cessation.

In my imaginings and within dreams, deluded by the madness of longing, I see that person. And so it was, dear friend; for a moment he gazed intently at me, his eyes like white lotuses dancing with a wild, trembling motion as they were upturned in wonder and agitated, appearing as if reeling from the intoxication of matured maireya wine. (28)

"I see him, and he, as it were, sees me. How so? Therefore, there are two adverbs: first, "excessively" (*udbhaṭam*), meaning with the dancing of eyes that for a moment become upturned through astonishment and fainting; and second, "as if having the habit of reeling from the intoxication of wine. (29) *Udvellam*: blossomed, with a knitting of the eyebrows. (30) *Uppehaḍaṃ*: excessively. (31) *Ṅijjhāedi*: he gazes intently.

Moreover, O beloved Madayantika, he speaks while filling the cavities of my ears with a deep and resonant *Bhārata* voice, faltering and gurgling like the cry of a swan whose throat has been reddened by swallowing the filaments of lotuses.
This gurgling and faltering occur first in the dream state as a form of imperfect articulation, caused by the influence of anxiety associated with the emerging state of pregnancy.
Furthermore, as if arising from the failure of her attempt to grasp the hem of his upper garment, he terrifies me, whose heart is throbbing and fluttering with agitation.

The word *atha* is used here as a conjunction (*samuccaye*), just like *api cet*. *Pahavantako* means "as if possessing power" (*prabhavann iva*); it has the sense of "like a master" (*patir yathā*). *Parābhava* refers to the state of being defeated due to a lack of effective action. *Sasaṃbhramam* means "with agitation" (*sasādhvasam*). *Uttaraṅgam* means "surging with waves" (*udgatakallolam*). *Dhamadhamāyamānam* means "throbbling" or "trembling. She whose heart is thus is described as such. Here, the "wave" (*kallola*) refers to the continuous and successive manifestation of trembling. *Uttrāsayati* means "she causes to be startled" or "makes her tremble with fear. (31)

She whose emergence of breasts was not able to be concealed—because, immediately after being suddenly released and cast away at that very moment, her arms, which were like the stalks of firm lotuses, remained covered with horripilation, and thus the [breasts] were bound by them. (32) By suddenly breaking off the embrace and moving far away, it becomes easy for the hero to gaze upon her pair of breasts and so forth.

The meaning is that the heroine was not able to conceal herself by that much. If she was unable to cover herself with her garment or other clothing, why did she not turn her back and flee? To this he says:
"Her thick thighs were restrained by her girdle and bracelets, which were loosened and rendered disordered as she attempted to move away in the opposite direction. [00]

"Vighaṭamāna" means expanding in its knots due to the manifestation of horripilation, arising from the nourishment of an excess of joy congealed at the moment of embracing. "Vihvala" means wavering from one's natural state. "Saṃdānyamāna" means being led toward the yoke of bondage.

He mocks me—even though I am acting contrary to his will, my heart made harsh by the pain of a momentary outburst of anger brought about by every kind of effort, yet whose entire essence of mind is revealed through my affectionate, repeatedly rolling eyes.

*Upahāsaḥ* (jesting): *parihāsaḥ* (mockery). When a heroine is being forcefully approached by the hero, her impudence and aversion indicate her timidity; thus, there is the introduction of her acting perversely through a momentary hardness produced by great effort. And because that jesting is not so charming when the heroine acts perversely, there is the introduction of her affectionate eyes turning again and again for the sake of gaining his confidence.

O dear friend, having rendered her motionless and constrained by the embrace of his two arms—arms that were like double-edged staffs—and having placed her upon his chest, which was adorned with the formidable patterns of the claws of a fully grown tiger and rendered helpless by their grip; and having, with trembling head, seized her disheveled braid with his hand and gathered her hair together, he held her face steady while her lotus-like mouth blossomed freely and artfully.

With his body’s beauty intensified by the overwhelming pleasure of the delightful touch of her lower lip—quivering and gathered together, long pressed against the root of his left cheek—he, driven by some reckless resolve suited to his ill-bred audacity, makes advances toward me, though I am not to be solicited.
My dear friend, having experienced all this in person, I, unfortunate as I am, shall suddenly perceive this world of the living once again as resembling a desolate wilderness.

A young woman, being approached for the first time by a man who has attained confidence and delights in immodesty, is said to be honored [in return] as follows: having drawn him close to her heart, she embraces him firmly with both arms, seizes his mass of hair with the fingers of her hands, and—keeping all the features of her face motionless—is courted by him through kisses upon her eyes, throat, cheeks, lower lip, and the interior of her mouth, while her lotus-like face blossoms with a smile.

And she, out of a sudden flurry caused by immediate timidity, strikes with her head—shaken with agitation—the hero’s hand which was intent on gathering her hair into a knot; she strikes it because of her weakness resulting from the hero’s firm embrace of her arms. *Oaggiaṃ* means "gathered" (referring to the hair and so forth), according to regional usage (*deśī*). The cleverness (*vaidagdhyam*) of her face arises from her skill in various kinds of kissing. *Uddharṣitam* means "with bristling hair" (*udgataromāñcam*).

And because he established all the ritual services (*upacāra*) on her left side, out of cleverness he made his request for sexual union at her left ear; thus it is said, "on the left cheek. The agitation (*saṃbhrama*)—the intense flurry—caused by the conflicting states of trepidation and bliss, results from the wavering of consciousness therein. Due to delusion (*moha*), that is, confusion regarding what ought to be done, there is sluggishness (*mantharatva*), which is the inability to settle upon either course: neither engaging in it due to the force of trepidation, nor withdrawing from it due to the surge of bliss. Then, "suddenly" (*jhagiti*): she has become fully awakened.
Lavaṅgikā: Friend Madayantikā, tell me clearly.
If the reading is *akkhesi*, it means "you will tell.

Now, at that moment, having been observed by the eyes of Buddharakṣitā—which were blossoming with a smile mixed with affection and agitation—you must ask the attendants whether your seat, the *āsūraka* (a type of cushion), or the bed-covering cloth, which ought to be concealed from view, is there or not.

The *āsana* known as *masūraka* is commonly called *visārī*. Because of the previous mention of the plural form in the phrase "and in [the states of] resolve and dreams," it is implied that sometimes, even while seated, a female attendant—her body rendered incapable of enduring separation due to exhaustion and other factors—enters into that state; thus, there is skill in posing questions regarding the emission of the final element (*caramadhātu*) even in the case of the *masūraka* posture.

And here, because the lack of prominence of Makaranda is indicated by the description of his lineage and other qualities—just as was done for Mādhava—it is suggested that Madayantikā alone is the object of such jesting, and thus she is not the principal heroine (*pradhānanāyikā*) here; for this *prakaraṇa*, being a work of another author’s composition, cannot tolerate the presence of multiple principal heroes.
(33) MADAYANTIKĀ: Oh you who are habituated to irrelevant joking, begone!
BUDDHARAKṢITĀ: Friend Madayantika, only a dear friend of Mālatī would know how to converse in such a manner.
[The intention is: "Because she has seen so many such forms in Mālatī herself, she imagines you to be like this as well"—thus, through this underlying thought, there is an introduction of confidence.
MADAYANTIKĀ: Friend, do not indeed mock Mālatī in this way.
